name: Alexander's campaign
traveler: Alexander of Macedon and his army
summary: A Macedonian army crosses into Asia, destroys the Persian empire and marches to the Indus. It brings surveyors (bematists) who pace out the roads, and its reports, together with Nearchus' voyage home along the coast, give the Greek world its first first-hand picture of Persia, Central Asia and India.

stops.note: The army, about 40,000 strong, leaves the Macedonian capital.
First victory over the Persian satraps after crossing into Asia.
Alexander cuts the Gordian knot, by the story.
Defeats Darius III, who flees east.
A seven-month siege of the island city.
Consults the oracle of Ammon in the desert.
Founds the city that will become the Greek world's centre of learning.
Decisive defeat of Darius.
The city opens its gates.
The palaces are looted and burned.
Darius is murdered by his own officers.
Two years of hard fighting in Bactria and Sogdiana.
Sogdian resistance under Spitamenes lasts two years.
'Alexandria the Furthest', on the Jaxartes.
The king of Taxila joins him.
Defeats King Porus and his elephants.
The army refuses to go on toward the Ganges, of which it has heard.
The Indus delta; first sight of the Ocean's tides.
A disastrous march through the desert; thousands die.
Nearchus brings the fleet along the coast from the Indus and finds Alexander inland.
Mass weddings of Macedonians and Persians.
Alexander dies, aged 32, planning a voyage around Arabia.

informs.note: The Ganges and the Gangaridai, by report

name: Amundsen to the South Pole
summary: Amundsen lets his crew believe they are bound for the Arctic, then turns south. With dogs, skis and four companions he reaches the South Pole five weeks before Robert Falcon Scott, whose party dies on the way back.

stops.note: The Fram leaves; the crew think they are bound for the Arctic.
Amundsen tells the crew the real goal and cables Scott: 'Beg leave to inform you Fram proceeding Antarctic.'
Winter base on the Ross Ice Shelf. On 20 October five men set out with four sledges and 52 dogs.
They climb a glacier to the polar plateau and kill most of the dogs to feed the rest.
They reach the pole and leave a tent, Polheim, with letters for King Haakon and for Scott.
Back at base, 99 days after setting out.
The news is cabled to the world.

informs.note: First people at the South Pole
The news reaches Europe from Hobart

name: Apollo 11
traveler: Neil Armstrong, Buzz Aldrin and Michael Collins
summary: Eight days, 1.5 million kilometres, and the first people to walk on another world. Collins circles the Moon alone while Armstrong and Aldrin spend about two and a half hours outside on the surface.

stops.note: A Saturn V lifts off at 13:32 UTC.
One and a half orbits, then the third stage fires toward the Moon over the Pacific.
Apollo 11 slips into orbit behind the Moon, out of radio contact.
At 20:17 UTC: 'The Eagle has landed.'
At 02:56 UTC Armstrong steps onto the surface; Aldrin follows.
Eagle lifts off and rejoins Collins in Columbia.
The USS Hornet recovers the crew.

informs.note: The first people on another world

name: The voyage of the Beagle
summary: A Royal Navy survey ship sent to chart the coasts of South America takes along a 22-year-old naturalist. FitzRoy's charts were used for a century; Darwin's notes on fossils, finches and coral reefs led, more than twenty years later, to On the Origin of Species.

stops.note: Sails on a five-year voyage.
Darwin's first look at the geology of a volcanic island.
The tropical forest; Darwin is horrified by slavery.
Fossils of giant extinct ground sloths.
Three Fuegians brought to England on an earlier voyage are returned home.
Two years charting the coast of Patagonia.
Darwin crosses the Andes and finds sea shells near the summits.
An earthquake raises the coast by metres before his eyes.
Five weeks among tortoises and mockingbirds that differ from island to island.
A stop on the voyage.
Darwin is unimpressed by the colonists.
The colony impresses him; the bush does not.
Darwin works out how coral atolls grow on sinking volcanoes.
Meets the astronomer John Herschel.
Home after almost five years.

name: HMS Challenger
traveler: Charles Wyville Thomson, John Murray and the crew of HMS Challenger
summary: The first great oceanographic expedition sails 127,000 km, stopping every 200 miles to sound the depth, dredge the floor and take the temperature of the water. It finds over 4,000 new species, maps the Mid-Atlantic Ridge and sounds a trench near Guam deeper than any then known.

stops.note: A warship with most of its guns removed to make room for laboratories.
First deep soundings.
Soundings across the Atlantic reveal a ridge down its middle.
A stop to rest, resupply and take soundings.
A stop to rest, resupply and take soundings.
A stop to rest, resupply and take soundings.
Dredging the cold southern waters.
The first steamship to cross the Antarctic Circle.
A stop to rest, resupply and take soundings.
A stop to rest, resupply and take soundings.
A stop to rest, resupply and take soundings.
A stop to rest, resupply and take soundings.
A sounding of about 8,200 metres: the deepest water then known. The deepest part is later named after the ship.
A stop to rest, resupply and take soundings.
A stop to rest, resupply and take soundings.
A stop to rest, resupply and take soundings.
A stop to rest, resupply and take soundings.
A stop to rest, resupply and take soundings.
Home after 1,000 days; the results take 19 years and 50 volumes to publish.

informs.note: The first profile of the ocean floor

name: Columbus, first voyage
summary: Looking for a westward route to Asia, Columbus reaches the Bahamas, Cuba and Hispaniola, islands long home to the Lucayan and Taíno peoples. He thinks he is in the Indies. His printed letter spreads the news across Europe within months.

stops.note: 3 August: three ships, the Santa María, the Pinta and the Niña.
The last port before the open ocean.
Landfall on an island its Lucayan people call Guanahani; Columbus names it San Salvador.
He wonders whether this is the Asian mainland and sends envoys inland to find the Great Khan.
Larger islands, gold ornaments and the Taíno chief Guacanagarí.
The Santa María runs aground on Christmas Day; 39 men are left behind in a fort built from her timbers.
Sets out for Spain.
After a great storm, the Portuguese briefly arrest part of the crew.
Another storm drives the Niña into Lisbon; Columbus meets King João II.
Home.
Received by Ferdinand and Isabella. His letter is printed and spreads across Europe.

name: Cook's first voyage, with Tupaia
summary: Sent to Tahiti to watch Venus cross the Sun, the Endeavour takes aboard Tupaia, a Raʻiātean navigator and priest. His chart of the islands around Tahiti puts two ways of knowing the Pacific on one sheet of paper. Cook charts Aotearoa and eastern Australia; Tupaia dies at Batavia.

stops.note: The Endeavour sails for the Pacific.
Wine and onions against scurvy.
The Portuguese viceroy suspects them of smuggling.

stops.place: Bay of Good Success, Tierra del Fuego
stops.note: Banks and Solander collect plants; two men die of cold in a snowstorm.
The transit of Venus is observed on 3 June.
Tupaia, navigator and priest from Raʻiātea, joins the ship and pilots it through the islands.
Tupaia directs them south.
Tupaia can speak with Māori. The first meetings end in killings.
A transit of Mercury is observed; Cook charts the coast as he goes.
Cook sails around both islands, showing they are not part of a southern continent.
The Gweagal people resist the landing. Tupaia cannot understand their language.
The ship strikes the Great Barrier Reef and is beached for seven weeks of repairs.
Cook claims the east coast for Britain.
Repairs, malaria and dysentery. Tupaia dies here in December.
Dozens of the crew have died of fever since Batavia.
A last call on the British island before home.
Home with Tupaia's chart, thousands of specimens and new coastlines.

informs.note: News of Tupaia's meetings with Māori reaches Tahiti on Cook's second voyage

name: Cortés and the fall of Tenochtitlan
traveler: Hernán Cortés, Malintzin and their Tlaxcalan allies
summary: A few hundred Spaniards land on the Gulf coast, gain thousands of Indigenous allies who resent Mexica rule, and march on Tenochtitlan. With smallpox spreading ahead of them, they destroy the city after a long siege. Cortés's letters to Charles V put Mexico on Europe's map.

stops.note: Cortés sails against the governor's orders with eleven ships.
Finds Gerónimo de Aguilar, a shipwrecked Spaniard who speaks Maya.
After a battle, Malintzin is given to the Spaniards; speaking Nahuatl and Maya, she becomes the indispensable interpreter.

stops.place: Villa Rica de la Vera Cruz
stops.note: Founds a town to claim authority from the Crown and scuttles his ships.
After fierce fighting, the Tlaxcalans, enemies of the Mexica, become allies.
A massacre of the city's people.
Moctezuma receives them in a city of perhaps 200,000 on its lake.
Driven out on the Noche Triste, the Spaniards retreat to their allies. Smallpox spreads through Mexico.
After a 75-day siege the city falls and is razed; Mexico City is built on its ruins.

informs.note: Cortés's letters to Charles V, printed from 1522

name: Vasco da Gama
summary: Four Portuguese ships sail around Africa and, guided across the Arabian Sea by a pilot from Malindi, reach Calicut. The sea route joins Europe's map to an Indian Ocean world that Arab, Indian and Swahili sailors had long known.

stops.note: Four ships leave Restelo.
Water and meat before the open ocean.
A great arc far out to sea to find the westerlies: about three months without sight of land, the longest such passage Europeans had yet made.
First meetings with the Khoikhoi.
Rounded on 22 November.
Music and dancing with the Khoikhoi, then a quarrel over water.
Named on Christmas Day.
The first Swahili port. The sultan takes the Portuguese for Muslims, then turns hostile.
A hostile reception.
The sultan, Mombasa's rival, provides a pilot who knows the monsoon route.
India. Asked what they want, a crewman answers: 'Christians and spices.'
A three-month crossing against the wind. Scurvy kills many of the crew.
Rounded again, homeward.
Home with pepper and news. Two of the four ships and about a third of the men return.

name: The settlement of East Polynesia
summary: After a long pause in West Polynesia, double-hulled canoes sail east into the trade winds and, within a few centuries, find almost every habitable island across a triangle bigger than any continent. It is the last great human expansion into empty land. Dates come from radiocarbon and genetics and carry wide error bars.

stops.note: Canoes set out eastward, into the trade wind, so that a voyage that finds nothing can always run home.
Central East Polynesia is reached. Raʻiātea later becomes the sacred centre of voyaging.
Low atolls, hard to see from a canoe, are found and settled.
High islands to the north-east.
Mangareva, Pitcairn and Henderson become linked by a trade in stone tools.
Polynesians and Native Americans meet. Exactly where is unknown; the genetic signal points to this coast. The kūmara (sweet potato) spreads across Polynesia.
The most remote inhabited island on Earth, 2,000 km from its nearest neighbour.
A voyage of 3,800 km north across the equator, steering by stars that change as you go.
The southern Cook Islands.
A stepping stone in the Kermadecs.
The great southern islands, colder and larger than any yet found. The early site at Wairau Bar is shown here.

name: Hillary and Tenzing Norgay on Everest
summary: A British expedition led by John Hunt, carried by hundreds of porters and Sherpa climbers, puts two men on the highest point on Earth: Tenzing Norgay, a Sherpa, and Edmund Hillary, a beekeeper from New Zealand.

stops.note: The expedition sets out on foot with some 350 porters.
The heart of Sherpa country.
Weeks of acclimatization below the monastery.
A route is forced through the Khumbu Icefall.
Tom Bourdillon and Charles Evans turn back about 100 metres below the summit.
At 11:30 Hillary and Tenzing stand on the summit. The news reaches London on the morning of the coronation, 2 June.

name: Faxian's pilgrimage
summary: A Buddhist monk in his sixties walks to India for the monastic rules, then comes home by sea through Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia, and is blown far off course to the Shandong coast. His short record is the first Chinese account of the sea route from India.

stops.note: Sets out with four companions.
Crosses the desert, 'with only the bones of the dead to mark the way'.
A grand Buddhist procession.
Over the Pamirs into Gandhara.
A great centre of Buddhist sculpture.
Three years copying texts in the Gupta capital.
Takes ship for the Lion Kingdom.
Two years in Sri Lanka; seeing a fan from China, he weeps with homesickness.
A storm drives the ship to an island where 'heretics and Brahmins flourish'.
Bound for Guangzhou, the ship is blown north for months and lands on the Shandong coast.
Writes the Record of Buddhist Kingdoms.

name: Gagarin, Vostok 1
summary: A 27-year-old Soviet pilot makes one orbit of the Earth in 108 minutes. The line on the map is his ground track: the path traced on the surface beneath him.

stops.note: Lift-off at 09:07 Moscow time. 'Poyekhali!' ('Let's go!')
In orbit, climbing toward the most northerly point of the track.
Crossing the Pacific into the night side of the Earth.

stops.place: Near the tip of South America
stops.note: The southernmost part of the orbit.
The retro-rocket fires to bring the capsule down.
108 minutes after launch Gagarin ejects and comes down by parachute in a field.

name: Hanno the Navigator
summary: A Carthaginian fleet sails out past the Pillars of Heracles to found colonies down the Atlantic coast of Africa, then explores further south. The account survives only in a short Greek translation, so how far Hanno got (Senegal, Sierra Leone or Cameroon) is still argued over.

stops.note: Sixty ships carrying colonists set out.
The first colony, beyond the Pillars of Heracles.
A wooded headland, where they build a shrine to Poseidon.
Friendly herders act as interpreters for the voyage south.
An island trading post, as far from the Pillars as Carthage is.
A river full of crocodiles and hippopotamuses: perhaps the Senegal.
At night they see fires and hear pipes and drums from the land.
A great burning mountain: perhaps Mount Kakulima in Guinea, or Mount Cameroon.
They capture three 'hairy people' their guides call gorillai, then turn back for want of supplies.

name: Humboldt and Bonpland in the Americas
traveler: Alexander von Humboldt and Aimé Bonpland
summary: A Prussian naturalist and a French botanist carry 42 instruments through the Spanish Americas, measuring altitude, temperature, magnetism and plants as they go. They show how climate and life change with height, and their thirty-volume account remakes Europe's picture of South America.

stops.note: Sail on the Pizarro with royal permission to go anywhere in Spanish America.
Climb the volcano and record how vegetation changes with height.
First landfall in America.
Experiments with electric eels on the grassy plains.
Confirm that the Casiquiare joins the Orinoco to the Amazon basin.
Studies the cinchona trees that give quinine.
Climbs the volcanoes around the city.
Reach about 5,900 metres, higher than anyone known before them; from it Humboldt draws his famous profile of life by altitude.
Measure the cold current offshore, later named after Humboldt.
By sea to New Spain.
A year in New Spain's archives and mines.
Meets President Jefferson, who wants news of Mexico's borders.
Home with 60,000 specimens; publishing takes thirty years.

name: Ibn Battuta
summary: A young legal scholar from Tangier sets out for Mecca and keeps going for 29 years, across some 120,000 km of the Islamic world and beyond it. Back in Fez he dictates the Rihla. A few of its episodes, such as the visit to the Volga, are doubted by scholars.

stops.note: Leaves home at 21 'to make the pilgrimage'. He will be gone 24 years.
Two envoys of the sultan of Tunis join him on the road.
Falls ill with fever and ties himself to his saddle to keep going.
Joins a pilgrim caravan.
Travels with a caravan for safety against raiders.
The great lighthouse is still partly standing.
'Mother of cities', the largest city he has seen.
The Red Sea crossing is blocked, so he goes north through Syria.
Visits the tomb of the Prophet.
His first hajj.
The shrine of Ali.
Shocked to hear the preacher's grammar mistakes in the Friday sermon.
Much of the city in ruins after feuds between factions.
Meets the city's famous ascetic, Majd al-Din.
Still recovering from the Mongol sack of 1258.
The bazaar of the jewellers.
Stays to study.
Takes ship south.
Hot, waterless and rich.
Describes the sultan's court and its enormous meals.
An island town where bananas, lemons and fish are the staple food.
'One of the most beautiful and best-built towns', its houses of wood.
Frankincense and horses for India.
The new island city, rich from the Indian trade.
His third hajj.
Anatolia's Turkish principalities welcome him at every town.
Takes ship across the Black Sea.
A Genoese port; he is alarmed by its church bells.
The moving camp and capital of Özbeg Khan of the Golden Horde.
Escorts the Khan's Byzantine wife, Princess Bayalun, on a visit home.
Its mosques and colleges still damaged from the Mongols.
'One of the greatest and finest cities', though many palaces lie in ruin.
Still in ruins after Genghis Khan.
Crosses the Hindu Kush, which he says means 'slayer of Indians'.
Reaches the Indus.
Serves as a judge under Sultan Muhammad bin Tughluq for eight years.
Sent as envoy to China; the junks are wrecked in a storm before he boards.
Becomes a judge, marries into the ruling family and leaves after a quarrel.
Climbs to the footprint at the summit.
Cheap rice and fruit; he calls it 'a hell full of good things'.
A Muslim sultan gives him a junk for China.
'One of the greatest ports in the world, or rather the greatest.'
A city so big it takes three days to cross.
Leaves China.
Back on the long sea road west.
Last sight of India.
Frankincense and horses for India.
Passes through on the way west.
The Black Death kills thousands a day.
His last hajj.
Back in the city where his travels first impressed him.
The last stage before home.
Home. His mother has died of the plague a few months before.
Visits al-Andalus.
Sets out across the Sahara.
A town whose houses and mosque are built of salt slabs.
He is offended by the governor's manners, and surprised that women here go unveiled.
Eight months at the court of Mansa Sulayman, Musa's brother. The city's site is still uncertain.
Sees the tomb of the poet es-Saheli.
'One of the finest towns in the land of the Sudan.'
A copper-mining town.
Called home by the sultan, who sets the scholar Ibn Juzayy to write down his story.

name: Ibn Fadlan's embassy to the Volga
summary: Secretary of an Abbasid embassy to the king of the Volga Bulghars, Ibn Fadlan crosses the frozen steppe of the Oghuz Turks and writes the most vivid early description of the Rus, including a ship burial.

stops.note: The embassy leaves the caliph's court.
Through the Zagros by the old Khorasan road.
Rayy, near today's Tehran.
The great city of Khorasan.
Received by the Samanid emir.
Winter so cold that beards freeze to blocks of ice.
Among the Oghuz Turks, whose customs he describes with curiosity and disapproval.
Crossing the rivers on rafts of camel skin.
Meets the Volga Bulghar king, and the Rus traders, whose chieftain's ship burial he witnesses.
Returns; his report (the Risala) is written down.

informs.note: The homeland of the Rus, by report

name: Leif Erikson to Vinland
summary: Norse Greenlanders sail west and winter in a land of grapes and timber. The knowledge stays in the sagas of the far north, reaches the rest of Europe as a rumour in Adam of Bremen, and fades. Five centuries later the Americas have to be found again.

stops.note: Leif buys the ship of Bjarni Herjólfsson, who had sighted land to the west, and sets out with 35 men.
'Land of flat stones': probably Baffin Island.
'Land of forests': probably Labrador.
They winter where there are grapes and timber. The Norse site at L'Anse aux Meadows, found in 1960, fits the sagas.
Home with timber and grapes. Later voyages try to settle, then give up.

informs.note: Known in Greenland and Iceland; reaches the rest of Europe through Adam of Bremen, c. 1075

name: Lewis and Clark's Corps of Discovery
traveler: Meriwether Lewis, William Clark, Sacagawea and York
summary: A U.S. Army company sent by Jefferson to find a water route to the Pacific and to map the lands bought from France. Guided and helped by many Native nations, among them the Shoshone woman Sacagawea, they reach the Pacific and come back with maps, specimens and the news that no easy route exists.

stops.note: About 45 men start up the Missouri.
First council with Oto and Missouria leaders.
Winter among the Mandan and Hidatsa; Sacagawea and Toussaint Charbonneau join.
A month to haul the boats around the falls.
They cross the Continental Divide; the Shoshone chief turns out to be Sacagawea's brother.
Near starvation crossing the Bitterroot Mountains in snow.
The Nez Perce feed them and keep their horses.
'Ocian in view! O! the joy.' Winter on the Pacific coast.
Back after 28 months, long given up for dead.

name: Livingstone crosses Africa
traveler: David Livingstone and his Makololo companions
summary: A Scottish missionary-doctor, with men lent by the Makololo chief Sekeletu, walks from the upper Zambezi to the Atlantic, then back across the whole continent to the Indian Ocean. Along the way he is shown Mosi-oa-Tunya, which he names Victoria Falls.

stops.note: Sekeletu provides 27 men for the journey west.
Fever almost every week.
Reaches the Atlantic, exhausted, and turns back to bring his companions home.
Back with his companions, as promised, a year later.
'The smoke that thunders.' He names it after his queen.
A Portuguese outpost on the lower Zambezi.
The Indian Ocean: the first recorded crossing of southern Africa by a European.

name: Magellan–Elcano
traveler: Ferdinand Magellan and Juan Sebastián Elcano
summary: Five ships set out to reach the Spice Islands by sailing west. Magellan finds the strait at the tip of South America and dies in the Philippines; Elcano brings one ship and eighteen men home. The voyage reveals how vast the Pacific is.

stops.note: Five ships and about 270 men.
Last supplies in the Canaries.
Rest and fresh food from the Tupi people.
They search the estuary for a passage west and find only fresh water.
Winter. A mutiny is crushed; one ship is wrecked scouting the coast.
The entrance to the strait.
Three ships come out into an ocean Magellan names the Pacific. A fourth has deserted.
An uninhabited atoll. For months the crew have eaten biscuit dust, rats and leather; many die of scurvy.
Food and water from the Chamorro people, then a violent clash.
The Philippines.
Rajah Humabon and hundreds of his people are baptized.
Magellan is killed fighting the warriors of Lapulapu.
A great court with elephants.
The Spice Islands at last. They load cloves.
The Victoria sails on alone under Elcano; the Trinidad stays behind and is lost.
Elcano keeps far south to avoid Portuguese ships.
Rounded after weeks of storms.
Thirteen men sent ashore for food are seized by the Portuguese.
The Victoria returns with 18 men, the first ship to sail around the world.

name: Mansa Musa's hajj
summary: The king of Mali crosses the Sahara to Mecca with a caravan of thousands and so much gold that its price in Cairo stays low for years. Cairo's chroniclers write Mali into the Islamic world's geography, and within fifteen years a crowned African king appears on Mediterranean charts.

stops.note: The caravan leaves the capital of Mali. Niani is one candidate for its site; the capital has not been located for certain.
The last town before the desert.
Oases of the central Sahara.
He gives away and spends so much gold that its value in Cairo falls for years, al-Umari reports.
Performs the hajj.
Out of money, he borrows from Cairo's merchants at high interest for the journey home.
Mali's general has taken Songhay's capital; Musa visits.
Commissions the Djinguereber mosque, said to be designed by the Andalusian poet Abu Ishaq es-Saheli.
Home.

informs.note: 'Rex Melly' appears on Dulcert's chart; the Catalan Atlas of 1375 shows Musa holding a gold nugget

name: Napoleon's expedition to Egypt
traveler: Bonaparte's army and the Commission of Sciences and Arts
summary: A French invasion of Ottoman Egypt that ends in military failure but brings along 167 scholars, engineers and artists. They measure, draw and collect everything, find the Rosetta Stone, and publish the Description de l'Égypte: the first systematic survey of a whole country outside Europe.

stops.note: Some 35,000 soldiers and 167 savants sail in secret.
Taken from the Knights of St John on the way.
The army lands and storms the city.
After the Battle of the Pyramids, the Institut d'Égypte is founded in the city.
Nelson destroys the French fleet; the army is stranded.
Desaix's column, with the artist Vivant Denon, reaches the temples of Upper Egypt.
The southern limit of the survey.
Soldiers find a stone inscribed in hieroglyphs, Demotic and Greek; it will unlock the hieroglyphs in 1822.
The Syrian campaign stalls at Acre; Bonaparte slips back to France in August.
The French surrender to the British; the Rosetta Stone goes to London, the notes to Paris.

name: Monsoon trade (the Periplus route)
summary: An anonymous merchant's handbook describes the ports from the Red Sea to India and down the African coast, and how ships cross open water on the seasonal winds. It is a route rather than a single voyage, so its stops are composite.

stops.note: Goods leave the capital of Roman Egypt up the Nile.
From the Nile, caravans cross the desert to the Red Sea ports.
Ships bound for India leave in July to catch the monsoon.
The port of Aksum: ivory and tortoiseshell.
An Arab market town near the straits.
Once the meeting point of Indian and Egyptian ships.
The Cape of Spices at the tip of the Horn.
Cinnamon, tortoiseshell and slaves on the Somali coast.
The last market town of Azania. Beyond it, the author says, the ocean is unexplored and curves round to the west.
Settled by Arab, Indian and Greek traders.
The frankincense harbour of Dhofar.
Port at the mouth of the Indus.
The busiest port of western India, with pilots to guide ships through its tides.
Pepper port of the Chera kingdom. Some ships sail here directly from Arabia on the monsoon.
The southern tip of India.
A market town on the east coast; Roman pottery has been dug up at nearby Arikamedu.
Known only by report, like Chryse beyond it and, far inland, Thinae, where silk is made.
Ships return on the north-east monsoon from November.

name: Marco Polo
summary: A Venetian merchant's son goes east at seventeen and comes home at forty-one. In a Genoese prison he dictates a book about Kublai Khan's empire, and that book carries Cathay, Quinsay and Cipangu onto European maps.

stops.note: Marco, aged 17, leaves with his father Niccolò and uncle Maffeo, who have been to China once already.
They collect holy oil from Jerusalem, as Kublai Khan had asked.
The port of Lesser Armenia.
Through Greater Armenia, past a mountain where Noah's ark is said to rest.
A great market of the Ilkhanate.
Turquoise mines and fine embroidery.
They find the ships sewn with coconut twine and too flimsy to trust, and turn back to go overland.
'A noble city', still in ruins from the Mongol conquest.
Marco falls ill and recovers in the mountain air over a year.
A high plain where fire burns poorly and wild sheep carry huge horns.
Gardens, vineyards and cotton.
Jade from its rivers.
A month to cross the desert, where voices are said to lure travellers off the road.
A Buddhist oasis at the desert's edge.
They stay a year on unexplained business.
Kublai's summer capital, with a cane palace held up by silk cords.
Marco enters the Khan's service and learns several languages.
Missions to the far south-west, towards Burma.
He claims to have governed the city for three years; Chinese sources do not mention him.
'The finest and noblest city in the world', with twelve thousand bridges.
Sails with fourteen ships escorting the princess Kököchin to her bridegroom in Persia.
A kingdom that pays tribute to the Khan in elephants.
Five months waiting for the monsoon; he calls Sumatra 'Java the Less'.
Rubies, and the mountain with Adam's footprint.
Pearl divers of the Gulf of Mannar.
Pepper and brazilwood.
Of the six hundred who sailed, a few dozen survive.
News arrives that Kublai Khan has died.
Robbed of part of their goods.
Through the Bosporus toward home.
Home after 24 years; their relatives do not recognize them.
Captured in a sea battle, he dictates his book in prison to Rustichello of Pisa.

informs.note: Cipangu, an island of gold, by report

name: Pytheas of Massalia
summary: A Greek astronomer sails out past the Pillars of Heracles, circles Britain and hears of Thule, an island six days north where the sea turns thick. His book is lost and later writers called him a liar, but the north never quite left the map again.

stops.note: Sets out from the Greek colony at the mouth of the Rhône.
Past the Pillars of Heracles and into the Ocean, a route Carthage tried to keep closed.
The far western tip of Gaul.
Visits the tin traders and describes how they carry tin to a tidal island to sell.
The northern headland of Britain.
Six days north lies Thule, where the summer night barely falls and the sea becomes a thick 'sea-lung'. Iceland, Norway and Shetland have all been proposed.
The southeastern corner of Britain; he estimates the island's whole circuit, roughly correctly.
An island he calls Abalus, where amber washes up in spring: perhaps Heligoland or the Jutland shore.
Home, perhaps overland by the rivers of Gaul. He writes On the Ocean, which survives only in the quotations of sceptics.

name: Trieste to the Challenger Deep
summary: Two men sealed inside a steel sphere slung beneath a float of gasoline sink nearly eleven kilometres to the floor of the Mariana Trench, the deepest point of the ocean. No one returns there for 52 years.

stops.note: The bathyscaphe Trieste is towed out by the USS Wandank.
At 08:23 Piccard and Walsh begin to descend.
At 13:06 they touch bottom at about 10,900 metres. An outer window has cracked on the way down. They report seeing a flatfish.
Back on the surface at 16:56, after nine hours.

informs.note: The deepest point of the ocean

name: Xuanzang's pilgrimage to India
summary: A young monk slips out of Tang China without permission to find better Buddhist texts. Sixteen years later he returns with 657 of them and dictates a record of 138 countries that maps India for China in detail.

stops.note: Leaves secretly; travel abroad has been forbidden.
Slips past the frontier guards at night.
Crosses the Gobi alone on an old red horse and nearly dies of thirst.
The first oasis beyond the desert.
The king of Gaochang begs him to stay and teach; he goes on hunger strike to be let go.
A Buddhist kingdom famous for its musicians.
Crosses the Tian Shan; many of his party die in the snow.
Received by the khagan of the Western Turks in his felt tent.
An oasis city on the road west.
A great trading city, not yet Buddhist.
The Nava Vihara monastery.
Sees the great standing Buddhas, then gilded.
Once a Buddhist heartland, now with many ruined monasteries.
Two years of study.
A centre of Buddhist sculpture.
Capital of King Harsha.
Birthplace of the Buddha, already in ruins.
The deer park at Sarnath where the Buddha first taught.
The tree of the enlightenment.
Studies under the abbot Silabhadra for five years.
A port where he hears of Sri Lanka but does not go.
The far south of his travels.
Harsha holds a great assembly in his honour.
Crosses the Pamirs; loses his elephant and many texts at a river crossing.
The western gate of the Tarim basin.
Writes to the emperor to ask pardon for having left.
Waits here for the emperor's reply.
Returns with 657 texts. Emperor Taizong asks him to write down everything he saw.

informs.note: The Great Tang Records on the Western Regions

name: Yermak's campaign across the Urals
summary: A band of Cossacks hired by the Stroganov merchants crosses the Urals and takes Qashliq, capital of the Khanate of Sibir. Yermak dies in an ambush, but Russia's advance across Siberia to the Pacific follows within sixty years.

stops.note: About 540 Cossacks set out by river boat.
They drag their boats over the watershed.
Down the Tura and Tobol into Sibir.
Firearms decide the battle against Khan Kuchum's army.
The capital of Sibir is taken.
Envoys bring Ivan IV furs and news of the conquest.
Yermak drowns during a night attack, weighed down, the story says, by his armour.

name: Zhang Qian's mission to the west
summary: Sent to find allies against the Xiongnu, Zhang Qian is captured twice and gone for thirteen years. He brings back no alliance, but his report opens Central Asia to Han China and starts the trade later called the Silk Road.

stops.note: Emperor Wu sends him west with about a hundred men to find the Yuezhi.
He leaves Han territory.
Captured by the Xiongnu and held for about ten years. He marries and has a son, but keeps the envoy's staff.
Escapes west. Dayuan has walled cities, grape wine and the 'blood-sweating' horses.
The people of Kangju guide him on to the Yuezhi.
The Yuezhi are settled and prosperous north of the Oxus and have no wish for revenge.
In the markets he sees bamboo and cloth from Shu, brought by way of a country called Shendu: India.
Returns along the southern rim of the Tarim basin.
Captured by the Xiongnu again while trying to pass through Qiang territory.
Escapes in the confusion after the Shanyu's death and reaches Chang'an with one companion, Ganfu, after thirteen years.

name: Zheng He's seven voyages
summary: Seven fleets of up to 250 ships carry Ming envoys, soldiers and goods across the Indian Ocean to Arabia and East Africa. Chinese sea knowledge reaches its peak, then the court stops the voyages and the routes fade from use. The route shown combines several voyages.

stops.note: The first fleet, with about 27,000 men, is assembled.
The fleet waits for the north-east monsoon.
The first port of call.
Majapahit. Some 170 of the fleet's men are killed in a local war.
Defeats the pirate chief Chen Zuyi and takes him to Nanjing.
Malacca becomes the fleets' depot and a Ming ally.
A sultanate at the northern tip of Sumatra.
Guli, 'the great country of the Western Ocean': the first voyage's goal.
Leaves a stone in Chinese, Tamil and Persian giving offerings to the Buddha, to a Hindu god and to Allah.
The fourth voyage reaches the great market at the mouth of the Gulf.
Adan: the king buys a giraffe and zebras to send to the emperor.
Mugudushu: houses of stone four or five storeys high, Fei Xin writes.
East African coast. Malindi's envoys had brought a giraffe to Nanjing in 1415.
The fifth fleet returns with envoys from seventeen countries.
On the seventh voyage, seven men including the interpreter Ma Huan travel from Calicut to Mecca.
Zheng He dies, probably at sea off this coast.
The last fleet comes home. No fleet like it is sent again.
